title: Closed-loop vs Open-loop Benchmarking Playbook
summary: A practical playbook comparing closed-loop (synchronous) and open-loop (asynchronous) load generation approaches for throughput benchmarks. Includes test matrix, warmup heuristics, repeatability controls, config templates, and a capture checklist tailored to LLM inference runtimes.
content:
Purpose:
This playbook codifies when to use closed-loop vs open-loop load generation for inference throughput experiments, how to configure each approach for comparable, repeatable results, and how to instrument runs to isolate bottlenecks. It is written for engineers running high-concurrency LLM benchmarks on Redwood’s serving runtime (hosted/dedicated/private).

Motivation / problem statement:
We regularly see discrepancies in measured throughput and latency depending on whether tests use closed-loop clients (clients that wait for each response before issuing the next request) or open-loop drivers (clients that continuously issue requests at a target rate). Differences arise from backpressure, queuing dynamics, connection handling, and client-side resource saturation. Teams need a reproducible methodology to choose the right generator and to make results comparable across experiments.

Definitions:
- Closed-loop: Each client coroutine issues a request and waits for a full response before issuing the next request. Emulates user-perceived latency and stateful clients.
- Open-loop: Client(s) issue requests independently of responses (rate-limited or burst-limited). Emulates load from many independent producers and stresses server queueing/dispatch.

High-level guidance:
- Use closed-loop when you care about tail latency under realistic concurrency (e.g., per-session traffic, interactive apps).
- Use open-loop when you need to stress dispatcher/queueing throughput and understand maximum sustainable token/sec under constant arrival rates.
- For SLAs that combine latency and throughput (e.g., 95th latency <= X under Y throughput), run both modes to detect graceful degradation/fallback behaviors.

Experiment matrix (recommended minimal set):
1) Baseline closed-loop sweep: Vary concurrent clients (8, 16, 32, 64, 128) with realistic prompt mix; measure p50/p95/p99 latency and aggregate token/sec.
2) Baseline open-loop sweep: Vary offered load (20%, 50%, 80%, 100% of expected max qps) with same prompt mix; track queue lengths, CPU/GPU utilization, and dropped requests.
3) Cross-check at cliff: Identify point where closed-loop throughput diverges from open-loop (usually due to device saturation or queueing); collect traces.
4) Repeatability runs: Run representative points 3× at different seeds/hour-of-day to quantify variance.

Warmup and priming heuristics (practical):
- Multi-stage warmup for both modes: 1) connection ramp (30–60s) to establish TCP/TLS tunnels and kernel caches, 2) brief low-rate primer (60–90s) to populate tokenizer/model caches and KV caches, 3) step ramp to target (2–5 minutes depending on scale).
- Avoid single-shot jumps to target rate; step ramps reduce oscillation and allow scheduler to stabilize.
- For closed-loop, ensure each client performs at least N=10 requests during warmup; that helps amortize JIT/first-token variance.
- For open-loop, perform a low-rate long primer (2–3 minutes) so KV/prefix caches settle; if using prefix cache invalidation tests, tag runs clearly.

Repeatability controls (must-haves):
- Fixed RNG seeds for any synthetic prompt sampling and client interarrival jitter.
- Capture and archive client-side loadgen configs (exact binary/version, runtime flags, concurrency settings).
- Pin model version and quantization profile in the experiment configuration.
- Record hardware allocation (instance types, GPU model, numa topology) and daemon process versions.
- Run each experiment at least 3 times and report mean and std; if stdev / mean > 0.05, investigate variance sources before claiming a delta.

Observability capture checklist (always collect):
- Server-side: CPU, GPU (util %, power draw), GPU SM occupancy, memory bandwidth counters, per-process token/sec, kernel-level context-switches, and thread-level latencies.
- Runtime internals: queue depth time series, scheduling latency (time from arrival to start-of-execution), KV cache hit/miss histogram, batched request sizes distribution, and batch-formation latency.
- Network: per-connection RTT, retransmits, socket backlog, and loadgen host NIC stats.
- Tracing: end-to-end traces with request IDs (client->front-end->worker), sampling at high rate for cliff runs.
- Client: request timers, concurrency observed, & any client-side errors/timeouts.

Failure modes to look for (examples and quick checks):
- Latency cliff in closed-loop but steady open-loop: indicates client-side queueing or connection reuse limits. Check per-client thread/async pool exhaustion and adjust client concurrency shape.
- Open-loop throughput plateau below expected: likely backpressure or resource fragmentation in the server scheduler; inspect batch-formation latencies and ``tiny batch`` ratio.
- Periodic spikes in p99: correlated with GC cycles, process restarts, or heavy background tasks (checkpointing, tracing uploads). Correlate p99 with system cron/ops events.

Config templates (example snippets you can copy)
- Closed-loop client config (YAML-like):
  mode: closed-loop
  clients: 64
  requests_per_client: 200
  inter_request_jitter: gaussian(mean=0, std=15ms)
  prompt_set_id: sample-mix-v2
  rng_seed: 12345
  transport: http2

- Open-loop client config (YAML-like):
  mode: open-loop
  offered_qps: 1200
  concurrency_limit: 1024
  burst_window_ms: 100
  prompt_set_id: sample-mix-v2
  rng_seed: 12345
  transport: http2

How to make closed/open comparisons fair:
- Match prompt-set and tokenizer distribution exactly (same seed and split).
- Align warmup duration and primer behaviors so caches are similar before measurement window.
- When comparing max throughput, use open-loop to find saturation then run closed-loop at concurrency corresponding to the same observed aggregated qps for latency comparison.

Short checklist for an experiment run (runbook):
- Step 0: Update experiment metadata sheet (commit id, model, quant, bin).
- Step 1: Provision clean test environment and verify no other workloads are present.
- Step 2: Start system monitors and tracing collectors.
- Step 3: Run warmup primer (connection + low-rate primer + step-ramp).
- Step 4: Execute steady-state measurement for configured window (recommended 6–10 minutes after warmup).
- Step 5: Stop collectors, archive raw traces and counter dumps, label artifacts with run metadata.
- Step 6: Repeat steps 1–5 two more times for repeatability.

Analysis tips (quick):
- Plot throughput vs p99 on same axis to reveal knee points; annotate with GPU util and batch sizes.
- Decompose variance by client-side vs server-side metrics: if server GPU util is low but throughput stalls, look at queueing and batch-formation.
- Use change-point detection on latency time-series to isolate transient degradations.

Notes and gotchas:
- Connection churn can masquerade as server instability—use persistent HTTP/2 connections for large closed-loop sweeps when possible.
- Tokenization cost: when prompt lengths vary, normalize results to token/sec rather than requests/sec.
- Internal caching behavior (tokenizer, KV cache) may require separate microbenchmarks to understand cold vs warm behavior.

Appendix: quick repeat-run template (copy into your run notes)
- run_id: <auto>
- date: <YYYY-MM-DD>
- mode: closed-loop | open-loop
- config_blob: <attached file>
- seed: <int>
- target: <qps or concurrency>
- warmup_duration: <s>
- steady_window: <s>
- notes: <free form>

If you have questions about this playbook or want a helper script to convert our legacy bench configs into the open/closed format, ping eng-serving-runtime or create JIRA-ENG-1428 and tag the run.
